# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Construction Spending, also referred to as Value of Construction Put in Place (VIP)

About the Survey

Purpose

To provide monthly estimates of the total dollar value of construction work done in the United States (including 50 states and the District of Columbia). The population of interest includes all private residential construction and improvements, nonresidential construction, and public construction.

Coverage

Construction work done each month on new structures or improvements to existing structures for private and public sectors (in 50 states and the District of Columbia).

Legal Authority and Confidentiality

Title 13, United States Code, Sections 131 and 182 authorizes the Census Bureau to conduct this collection and to request your voluntary assistance. By Section 9 of Title 13, United States Code, your report is confidential. It may be seen only by persons sworn to uphold the confidentiality of Census Bureau information, and may be used only for statistical purposes. The law also provides that copies of your report retained in your files are immune from legal process.

Primary Customers and Users

  • The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)
  • Other government agencies
  • Construction-related businesses

Products

The key statistics produced for Construction Spending are monthly estimates of the total dollar value of construction work done in the U.S. The survey covers construction work done each month on new structures or improvements to existing structures for private and public sectors (in 50 states and the District of Columbia). Data are shown by type of construction as seasonally adjusted annual rates and in unadjusted dollars.

Data on construction spending are available on a monthly and annual basis going back to 1993.

Statistics for construction are available at the U.S. level monthly, and by division, region, and state annually for selected categories. Private manufacturing is availalable monthly at the region and division level.

Construction spending estimates include the cost of labor and materials, architectural and engineering work, overhead, interest and taxes paid during construction, and contractor’s profits.

Construction work done each month on new structures or improvements to existing structures for private and public sectors (in 50 states and the District of Columbia).

Value of Construction Put in Place press releases are issued on the first working day of each month, 2 months after the reference month. Data are shown by type of construction in seasonally adjusted annual rate and unadjusted dollars.

Release and Revision Schedule

Preliminary value-in-place (VIP) estimates of the total dollar value of construction work done in the U.S. by private or public sector and type of construction are available in the Construction Spending press release according to the release schedule.

For value-in-place estimates of the total dollar value of construction work done, two months of data are revised along with the release of each month's preliminary estimates. An analysis of the VIP revisions for estimates is updated with the release of each year's preliminary May data. With the release of preliminary May data on the Construction Spending release, seasonally adjusted annual rates for the previous 88 months are also revised to reflect updated seasonal factors. Not seasonally adjusted monthly estimates of total construction spending by owner and type of construction category are also revised to reflect late reports and revised or new estimates from outside data sources.

Construction Spending

DEFINITIONS OF CONSTRUCTION

Construction includes the following:

1. New buildings and structures.

2. Additions, alterations, conversions, expansions, reconstruction, renovations, rehabilitations, and major replacements (such as the complete replacement of a roof or heating system).

3. Mechanical and electrical installations such as plumbing, heating, electrical work, elevators, escalators, central air-conditioning, emergency backup power, and other similar building services.

4. Site preparation and outside construction of fixed structures or facilities such as sidewalks, highways and streets, parking lots, utility connections, outdoor lighting, railroad tracks, airfields, piers, wharves and docks, telephone lines, radio and television towers, water supply lines, sewers, water and signal towers, electric light and power distribution and transmission lines, petroleum and gas pipelines, and similar facilities that are built into or fixed to the land.

5. Installation of the following types of equipment: boilers, overhead hoists and cranes, and blast furnaces.

6. Fixed, largely site-fabricated equipment not housed in a building, primarily for petroleum refineries and chemical plants, but also including storage tanks, refrigeration systems, etc.

7. Cost and installation of construction materials placed inside a building and used to support production machinery; for example, concrete platforms, overhead steel girders, and pipes to carry paint, etc. from storage tanks.

The following are excluded from construction:

1. Maintenance and repairs to existing structures or service facilities.

2. Cost and installation of production machinery and equipment items not specifically covered above, such as heavy industrial machinery, printing presses, stamping machines, bottling machines, and packaging machines; special purpose equipment designed to prepare the structure for a specific use, such as steam tables in restaurants, pews in churches, lockers in school buildings, beds or X-ray machines in hospitals, display cases and shelving in stores, and racks or servers in data centers.

3. Drilling of gas and oil wells, including construction of offshore drilling platforms; digging and shoring of mines (construction of buildings at mine sites is included); work that is an integral part of farming operations such as plowing and planting of crops.

4. Land acquisition.

VALUE OF CONSTRUCTION PUT IN PLACE

The “value of construction put in place” is a measure of the value of construction installed or erected at the site during a given period. For an individual project, this includes—

1. Cost of materials installed or erected.

2. Cost of labor (both by contractors and force account) and a proportionate share of the cost of construction equipment rental.

3. Contractor’s profit.

4. Cost of architectural and engineering work.

5. Miscellaneous overhead and office costs chargeable to the project on the owner’s books.

6. Interest and taxes paid during construction (except for state and locally owned projects).

The total value-in-place for a given period is the sum of the value of work done on all projects underway during this period, regardless of when work on each individual project was started or when payment was made to the contractors. For some categories, published estimates represent payments made during a period rather than the value of work actually done during that period. F

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Construction Spending
Description: Provides monthly estimates of the total dollar value of construction work done in the U.S. The data is collected through the Value of Construction Put in Place Survey (VIP) and covers construction work done each month on new structures or improvements to existing structures for private and public sectors.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Construction Spending: dataset research and preservation report

**Research date:** October 8, 2026  
**Authoritative publisher:** U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Department of Commerce  
**Also known as:** *Value of Construction Put in Place* (VIP); historically associated with the **C30** publication series.

## Executive assessment

**Your title and description are substantially correct.** Census explicitly describes the Value of Construction Put in Place Survey as providing monthly estimates of the dollar value of construction work performed in the United States on new structures and improvements to existing structures, for private and public sectors.[1]

Three qualifications are essential:

1. **Construction Spending is a statistical program and family of published estimates—not one raw survey file.** It combines project surveys, other federal surveys, administrative and industry sources, modeling, imputation, and benchmarking.
2. **“Spending” generally means the value of work installed or erected during the period**, not contract awards, appropriations, construction starts, or necessarily cash payments.
3. **The coverage is broad but not exhaustive.** Routine maintenance, land acquisition, and most production equipment are excluded. Estimates of improvements to rental, vacant, and seasonal residential properties were discontinued after a source survey lost funding.[2][3]

Its principal public value is as a timely measure of investment in buildings and infrastructure, including inputs to GDP estimates and economic policymaking. Its principal preservation challenge is that **historical estimates are repeatedly revised**, while classifications, coverage, and methods have changed.

---

## 1. Dataset identity and catalog-ready description

| Attribute | Verified description |
|---|---|
| Preferred title | Construction Spending |
| Alternate title | Value of Construction Put in Place |
| Acronym/program identifier | VIP |
| Historical publication identifier | C30 |
| Publisher | U.S. Census Bureau, Department of Commerce |
| Operational office | Economic Indicators Division, Construction Expenditures Branch |
| Methodological responsibilities | Economic Statistical Methods Division handles survey methodology and sample selection |
| Statistical status | Principal Federal Economic Indicator |
| Main measure | Dollar value of construction work performed during a reference period |
| Geographic universe | 50 states and District of Columbia |
| Main frequency | Monthly, with annual estimates and selected subnational products |
| Public observation unit | An aggregate estimate for a period, ownership/category, geography, and adjustment status |
| Underlying collection unit | Often a construction project; other components use household-survey or external-source information |
| Dollar basis | Current/nominal dollars in the contemporary series |
| Main adjustment variants | Not seasonally adjusted values and seasonally adjusted annual rates |
| Contemporary historical coverage | Monthly and annual series beginning in 1993 |
| Older predecessor coverage | Census maintains old-classification series for 1964–2002 |
| Access | Public tables, downloadable historical files, releases, charts, and Census API |
| Confidentiality | Identifiable survey responses protected under Title 13 |

Sources: Census program documentation, the Federal Register collection notice, and the supporting statement for the survey.[1][4][5][6]

### Recommended corrected description

> The U.S. Census Bureau’s Construction Spending program, also called Value of Construction Put in Place (VIP), publishes monthly and annual estimates of the current-dollar value of construction work performed in the 50 states and District of Columbia. It measures work on new structures and qualifying improvements to existing structures, classified by ownership and type of construction. Estimates combine Construction Progress Reporting Surveys, residential construction and expenditure sources, and other information, with statistical adjustments and revisions. Published products include unadjusted dollar values and seasonally adjusted annual rates.

This description avoids implying that every component is obtained directly from a single survey.

---

## 2. Publisher, authority, mandate, and governance

### Who produces it?

The **Census Bureau**, not the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), is the primary publisher.

The **Economic Indicators Division (EID)** plans and coordinates the project surveys, reporting forms, editing, tabulation, and publication. The **Economic Statistical Methods Division (ESMD)** is responsible for survey methodology and sample selection. The program’s public contact is the **Construction Expenditures Branch**.[5][14]

BEA is an important downstream user.

### Statutory authority

Census identifies **Title 13, United States Code, Sections 131 and 182** as authority to conduct the collection and request participation.[1]

**Participation in the Construction Progress Reporting Surveys is voluntary.** This is an important distinction: statutory authorization to operate the program does not make these survey responses compulsory.

### Confidentiality

**Title 13, Section 9** protects respondent information:

- Reports are used for statistical purposes.
- Access is limited to persons sworn to uphold Census confidentiality.
- Public responses may not identify a business, organization, or institution.
- Copies of reports retained by respondents are protected from legal process as described by Census.[1][6]

The public dataset is therefore an **aggregate statistical product**, not a public register of identifiable construction projects.

### Paperwork Reduction Act oversight

The core **Construction Progress Reporting Surveys (CPRS)** operate under:

- **OMB control number:** 0607-0153
- **Collection title:** Construction Progress Reporting Surveys
- **Current approval recorded in Reginfo:** approved August 18, 2025
- **Approval expiration:** August 31, 2028.[6]

The collection covers these forms:

| Form | Subject |
|---|---|
| C-700 | Private construction projects |
| C-700(R) | Multifamily residential projects |
| C-700(SL) | State and local government projects |
| C-700(F) | Federal government projects |

The current OMB inventory records **264,000 annual responses**, **51,333 annual burden hours**, and an estimated **$5.5 million annual federal cost**.[6]

**These figures concern the CPRS information collection, not necessarily the full cost or burden of every source used to produce Construction Spending.**

### Economic-indicator governance

Construction Spending is designated a **Principal Economic Indicator**. The survey’s supporting statement discusses evaluation under the federal statistical policy directive governing compilation, release, and evaluation of principal economic indicators; it reports an evaluation submitted to OMB in March 2022.[5]

I verified legal authorization, administrative oversight, and indicator status. I did **not** identify a separate dataset-specific statute prescribing every current table or requiring the present collection design in perpetuity.

---

## 3. What the estimates measure—and exclude

### The central concept: value put in place

VIP is the value of construction **installed or erected at the site during a given period**. For a project, it includes:

- Installed materials;
- Labor, including contractor and force-account labor;
- A proportionate share of construction-equipment rental;
- Contractor profit;
- Architectural and engineering work;
- Project overhead and office costs;
- Interest and taxes during construction, **except for state- and locally owned projects**.[2]

A multi-year project contributes to the estimates as work progresses. Its entire contract value is not counted in the month it begins.

Census also cautions that **some component estimates represent payments during a period rather than work physically completed during that period**.[2]

### Included construction

Examples include:

- New buildings;
- Additions, renovations, rehabilitation, reconstruction, conversions, and expansions;
- Major replacements, such as an entire roof or heating system;
- Plumbing, electrical, heating, elevators, and similar building services;
- Site preparation;
- Highways, utility lines, rail tracks, docks, airfields, and other fixed infrastructure;
- Certain specifically defined industrial installations and fixed, site-fabricated equipment.[2]

### Exclusions

Census excludes:

- **Routine maintenance and repairs**;
- **Land acquisition**;
- Most production machinery and specialized equipment;
- Oil and gas well drilling, including offshore drilling platforms;
- Mining excavation, although mine-site buildings are included;
- Work integral to farming operations, such as plowing and planting.[2]

A particularly useful contemporary distinction is that **data-center racks and servers are excluded equipment**, even though construction of the building and qualifying building systems may be included.

### Classification

Published statistics distinguish **private and public ownership**, with public estimates including federal and state/local components. Construction types include residential and categories such as manufacturing, commercial, office, lodging, education, health care, transportation, power, highways, water supply, and sewage/waste disposal.

Classification is primarily about **the structure’s intended use**, not simply the contractor’s industry. A Census API metadata label such as “Industry list” should not be taken to mean the construction categories are interchangeable with NAICS industry codes.

### Important interpretation limits

Construction Spending is **not**:

- Construction-industry value added;
- A count of projects or housing units;
- A stock measure of existing infrastructure;
- A permit, starts, or contract-award series;
- A measure of construction quality, accessibility, or need;
- A complete accounting of federal grants or infrastructure-law expenditures.

Nor does “public” mean “all construction financed in any way with public money.” Ownership and funding source are different dimensions.

---

## 4. How the data are produced

### A composite estimation system

The main components use different sources and methods.[3]

| Component | Main source or approach |
|---|---|
| Private nonresidential construction | Sampled project progress reports, coverage adjustments, and selected external sources |
| State/local public construction | Sampled project reports and category-specific coverage adjustments |
| Federal construction | Project reports, with adjustments or benchmarking to external agency information |
| New single-family construction | Survey of Construction information; estimated construction costs distributed across months using construction-progress patterns |
| New multifamily construction | Sampled multifamily projects and progress reporting |
| Residential improvements | Consumer Expenditure Survey information, with forecasts needed for timely monthly publication |
| Farm nonresidential construction | USDA annual information extrapolated into monthly estimates |
| Selected utility, railroad, and communications construction | Regulatory, industry, annual capital-expenditure, and other sources |

### Project sampling and follow-up

For private nonresidential and public projects, the methodology identifies **Dodge Data & Analytics** project lists as a principal sampling frame, supplemented with a small sample in areas without building-permit systems.

The project-list sampling unit includes projects valued at **$75,000 or more**. This threshold describes that sampling component; it should **not** be interpreted as meaning the published total intentionally excludes every smaller project.

The sample is stratified by ownership, construction type, and estimated project value. New projects enter monthly. Projects are followed through their construction progress.[3]

The current methodology describes approximately:

- **690** new private nonresidential projects selected monthly;
- **820** state/local projects;
- **60** federal projects;
- **220** multifamily projects.

These are **new-project selections**, not the total number of active projects reporting in a month. Earlier OMB documentation contains different counts; such operational figures must be dated rather than treated as permanent dataset attributes.

### Collected information

Key items include:

- Total construction cost;
- Construction start date;
- Completion date;
- Monthly value put in place;
- Architectural, engineering, and miscellaneous costs.

### Estimation and imputation

Reported project values are weighted and aggregated. The methodology includes adjustments for outliers, architecture/engineering costs, and duplicate frame entries.

Missing values are imputed. A project may have imputed total cost, start information, or monthly progress. Monthly imputations can be recalculated as additional information arrives, contributing to revisions.

Coverage adjustments are substantial:

- Private nonresidential estimates are increased **25%** for frame undercoverage.
- State/local adjustments differ by construction type.
- Federal estimates are adjusted to account for projects missing from the frame.[3]

These are part of the published estimation system, not errors discovered in individual records.

### Benchmarking

Private manufacturing construction is periodically benchmarked to **Annual Capital Expenditures Survey (ACES)** detailed structures information. Census lists benchmark years **1992, 1994, 1998, 2003, 2008, 2012, and 2017**, with carry-forward or extrapolation methods between benchmark years.[1][3]

Some other components depend on external annual data that become available one or two years after the reference period.

**Consequently, “monthly” describes the output frequency—not uniformly monthly direct observation of every component.**

---

## 5. History and consequential changes

| Period/date | Verified development | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1964–2002 | Census retains predecessor data under the old construction classification system | Historical coverage extends earlier than 1993 |
| Beginning in 1993 | A generalized classification based on end use was introduced for private nonresidential and state/local projects | Categories may not map directly to older building/nonbuilding classifications |
| January 2002 | Detailed project-level federal construction collection began | Federal-source methodology changed |
| August 1, 2003 | Census stopped publishing the old classification and constant-dollar series | Contemporary data should not be assumed to include an official real-dollar counterpart |
| Before 2008 | Residential improvements included rental, seasonal, and vacant properties through SORAR | Older coverage was broader |
| 2008 onward | Survey of Residential Alterations and Repairs (SORAR) discontinued because of budget cuts; no replacement source was available for those estimates | A documented loss of statistical coverage |
| Recent experimental expansion | Monthly subnational private-manufacturing estimates introduced, with an initial history beginning January 2017 | More frequent geographic detail, but different quality status |
| 2023 | Supporting documentation reports implementation of new certainty sampling strata | Sampling design is evolving |
| 2025–2028 | Current CPRS OMB approval period | Useful governance and renewal metadata |

Sources: methodology, predecessor-series pages, and experimental-product documentation.[3][5][7][8][9]

### Historical caveat

The earliest predecessor data I verified on the Census site begin in **1964**. That establishes available historical coverage; it does **not** conclusively establish the original inception date of every predecessor construction-statistics activity.

### Comparability resources

Census preserves both:

- Previous **1993–2007** series including rental/vacant/seasonal residential improvements; and
- Comparison series excluding those improvements.[8]

These are important preservation assets. A long-run analyst should not simply splice whichever files are easiest to download.

---

## 6. Release schedule, revisions, and versions

### Publication timing

Census describes releases as occurring on the **first working day of the month, two calendar months after the reference month**—for example, August activity published at the beginning of October.[1]

This is roughly one month after the reference month ends, not a full two-month wait after its end. The published release calendar should control, particularly when disruptions occur.

### Revisions

Census’s documented schedule includes:

- Revision of the **two preceding months** with each preliminary monthly release;
- Annual revisions accompanying preliminary **May** estimates;
- Revision of seasonal factors for the preceding **88 months**;
- Revisions to unadjusted figures for late reports and updated outside sources;
- Preliminary annual estimates with the December release;
- Finalization of the most recent two annual estimates with the following May-data release;
- Occasional unplanned revisions.[1]

### Why versions are central

A value for a particular month has at least two dates:

1. **Reference date:** when the construction occurred;
2. **Release/vintage date:** when that estimate became available.

For preservation and reproducible research, both must be retained.

A current historical spreadsheet answers, “What is Census’s latest estimate?” A contemporaneous release answers, “What did users know at that time?” Those are different research objects.

---

## 7. Quality, uncertainty, and methodological risks

### Sampling uncertainty

Census publishes sampling-variability information for applicable estimates and describes stratified-jackknife variance estimation. Its documentation explains **90% confidence intervals** using approximately **1.645 standard errors**.[3]

Sampling uncertainty does not capture all uncertainty. Coverage errors, respondent interpretation, imputation assumptions, external-source delays, and processing errors remain relevant.

A missing standard error is **not** proof of error-free measurement.

### Response and imputation

The methodology’s reported **2025 average unit response rates** include:

| Component | Unit response rate |
|---|---:|
| Private nonresidential | 17.9% |
| State/local public | 56.2% |
| Multifamily | 11.1% |
| Residential improvements | 58.0% |
| Federal | 52.0% |

The same documentation reports average imputation rates of **77.8% for private nonresidential**, **38.6% for state/local**, and **72.9% for new private multifamily** construction.[3]

These are significant quality indicators. However:

- Unit response and dollar-weighted response are different measures.
- Monthly progress response is different from obtaining initial project cost or dates.
- The rates should not be translated directly into a claim that the same fraction of all U.S. construction is “unknown.”

The OMB supporting statement identifies refusals and declining participation as persistent challenges and discusses research into phased spending models, alternative data, and satellite imagery.[5] These are **research directions**, not evidence that all such approaches are already operational.

### Other risks

- **Frame dependence:** A commercial project database is an important upstream dependency.
- **Coverage-adjustment age:** Census acknowledges that fixed-period coverage studies may not reflect changes in current undercoverage.
- **Residential improvement forecasts:** Source data arrive too late for complete direct monthly estimates, causing uncertainty and revisions.
- **Large-project concentration:** A small number of very large projects can materially affect detailed categories.
- **Experimental subnational estimates:** Census warns that these may not meet all statistical quality standards and are subject to disclosure thresholds.[9]

**Assessment:** The series is valuable for macroeconomic monitoring, but detailed monthly movements should be interpreted with uncertainty and revision history—not as precise project-level facts.

---

## 8. Users and public benefits

### Documented users

The Federal Register identifies these uses:[4]

| User | Use |
|---|---|
| BEA | Construction components of gross private domestic investment and GDP |
| Federal Reserve Board | GDP prediction and information relevant to monetary policy |
| Treasury Department | Economic forecasting |
| Other government agencies | Economic-policy evaluation |
| Construction businesses and trade associations | Market research |
| Materials producers and distributors | Estimating demand and scheduling production, distribution, and sales |

Researchers, journalists, investors, labor organizations, and civic groups can also use the published series, though the sources reviewed do not enumerate every such user group.

### Public benefits

The data support:

- **Economic transparency:** A public measure of investment activity, independent of individual firms’ promotional claims.
- **Better national accounts:** More informed GDP and investment estimates.
- **Policy monitoring:** Tracking construction in sectors such as schools, transportation, power, and manufacturing.
- **Business planning:** Matching materials and capacity to demand.
- **Historical research:** Studying development, investment cycles, and changing public/private construction patterns.
- **Public debate:** Testing broad claims that construction is expanding, contracting, or shifting among sectors.

### What activists should not infer

An increase in dollars does not necessarily mean:

- More physical infrastructure;
- Better infrastructure;
- More affordable housing;
- More equitable investment;
- More jobs;
- Successful implementation of a particular law.

Inflation, construction mix, geographic aggregation, and ownership classification all affect those interpretations.

---

## 9. Access, formats, API, and licensing

### Main access routes

| Resource | Purpose |
|---|---|
| [Program homepage](https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/c30index.html) | Authoritative starting point |
| [Data portal](https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/data/index.html) | Current products and downloads |
| [Historical data](https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/historical_data.html) | Contemporary historical series |
| [Previous series](https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/previousseries.html) | Discontinued coverage variants |
| [Old-classification data](https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/oldtc.html) | 1964–2002 predecessor series |
| [Historical release PDFs](https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/prpdf.html) | Contemporaneous releases |
| [Monthly subnational product](https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/monthlysubnational.html) | Experimental private-manufacturing estimates |
| [API documentation](https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/vip.html) | Programmatic access |

Current historical downloads include **XLSX** files. Older products include Excel, text tables, and PDF. The Economic Indicator Time Series system also offers search and chart functions.[7][10]

### API

The verified endpoint is:

```text
https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/vip
```

Important variables include:

- `category_code`
- `data_type_code`
- `cell_value`
- `seasonally_adj`
- `time`
- `time_slot_id`
- `time_slot_date`
- `time_slot_name`
- `geo_level_code`
- `error_data`
- `program_code`.[11]

The currently displayed API documentation says **data queries require an API key**.[12]

A documented example is:

```text
https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/vip?get=data_type_code,time_slot_id,seasonally_adj,category_code,cell_value,error_data&for=us:*&time=2012&key=YOUR_KEY_GOES_HERE
```

This is a documentation example, not a live extraction performed for this report. Preserve the code dictionaries and decode item/category types before analysis. The metadata declares `cell_value` as a string, so parsing requires deliberate numeric conversion and missing-value handling.

### Geographic availability

Census describes:

- National monthly statistics;
- Annual state, division, and region estimates for selected categories;
- Monthly region/division private-manufacturing estimates.[1]

**Do not assume every national category has a complete monthly state-level equivalent**, or that every website table is exposed through the same API endpoint.

### Secondary dissemination

The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis’s **FRED** republishes selected series, including total construction under **TTLCONS**. FRED identifies Census as the source.[13]

Secondary repositories are useful for access and cross-checking but should not replace Census definitions and revision documentation.

### Rights and confidentiality

Published Census-created federal statistical material is generally public-domain material under U.S. federal-work rules. I did not verify a dataset-specific Creative Commons license.

That does **not** make confidential responses public or confer redistribution rights over the proprietary upstream project database. Preserve any third-party notices accompanying source materials.

---

## 10. Guidance for data scientists

### Essential safeguards

1. **Distinguish SAAR from monthly dollars.**  
   A seasonally adjusted annual rate is an annualized pace. Do not sum twelve SAAR observations as annual spending. Use annual totals or sum appropriate unadjusted monthly amounts.

2. **Distinguish seasonal adjustment from inflation adjustment.**  
   Contemporary seasonally adjusted values remain nominal dollars. Real-growth analysis requires a defensible price index.

3. **Use consistent series definitions.**  
   Ownership, category, geography, adjustment status, and dollar units must agree.

4. **Do not double-count hierarchical categories.**  
   Totals and subcategories often appear together.

5. **Preserve missingness and suppression.**  
   A withheld or unavailable observation is not zero.

6. **Include release dates in forecasting data.**  
   Using revised historical values in a real-time backtest can introduce look-ahead bias.

7. **Account for historical breaks.**  
   Classification changes and residential-improvement coverage changes require explicit treatment.

8. **Check uncertainty before describing small movements.**  
   A point estimate rising does not necessarily demonstrate a statistically meaningful increase.

### Recommended analysis schema

```text
reference_period
release_date
retrieval_timestamp
source_url
program
ownership
construction_category_code
construction_category_label
geography_code
geography_label
frequency
seasonal_adjustment
annualization_status
dollar_basis
unit_multiplier
estimate
uncertainty_measure
publication_status_or_flag
methodology_version
```

Some of these fields are preservation metadata that users must add; they are not all supplied directly by the API.

---

## 11. Preservation and data-library priorities

### What to preserve

A strong archival package should contain:

- Original XLS/XLSX and text downloads;
- Monthly release PDFs;
- API responses and exact queries, excluding secret keys;
- Variable metadata and category/item dictionaries;
- Definitions and methodology documents;
- Survey forms and respondent instructions;
- Revision notices and annual revision analyses;
- Release calendars;
- Experimental-product quality statements;
- OMB supporting statements, approval records, and Federal Register notices;
- Prior classification and residential-coverage variants.

### Priority risks

**1. Overwritten historical estimates**  
Repeated revisions can erase the distinction between first release and latest estimate unless snapshots are retained.

**2. Lost semantic context**  
A preserved number without units, annualization, ownership, category definitions, and revision status is easily misused.

**3. Discontinued statistical coverage**  
SORAR’s cancellation demonstrates that useful parts of a federal statistical system can disappear. Archiving old observations preserves evidence but does not restore future coverage.

**4. Format and website fragility**  
Spreadsheet layouts, legacy links, PDFs, and metadata endpoints need independent capture and integrity checks.

**5. Upstream-source changes**  
Commercial frames and external annual data introduce dependencies outside the published series.

**6. Documentation drift**  
A stable methodology URL can serve a newer document. Preserve dated copies rather than the URL alone.

### Recommended archival practice

- Keep immutable **as-published** releases and a separate latest-revised collection.
- Record checksums, retrieval timestamps, filenames, and source URLs.
- Preserve originals alongside normalized CSV/Parquet derivatives.
- Version extraction code and classification crosswalks.
- Create a manifest linking each data release to its documentation.
- Store replicated copies in independently managed repositories.
- Assign a repository persistent identifier where possible.

For a librarian, the appropriate catalog object is often a **dataset collection with versioned distributions**, not a single static file.

---

## 12. Policy and historic-preservation applications

### Policy accountability

The data can help evaluate broad trends in public construction, sectoral priorities, manufacturing investment, and residential activity.

To attribute those changes to a particular law or grant program, supplement VIP with:

- Award and obligation records;
- Agency or recipient project reports;
- Local capital budgets;
- Permits and construction starts;
- Price measures;
- Employment and demographic information.

**VIP alone cannot identify which federal program financed a project or establish causal policy effects.**

Useful oversight questions include:

- Are coverage adjustments being reevaluated?
- How are declining response rates being addressed?
- Which source surveys are at funding risk?
- Are replacement data sources adequately tested?
- Are release vintages and methodology versions being retained?
- Is experimental geographic detail improving without concealing uncertainty?

### Historic-preservation research

For preservationists studying the built environment, qualifying rehabilitation and major renovations fall within the construction concept. But the dataset does **not** identify:

- Historic designation;
- Adaptive reuse;
- Demolition;
- Preservation tax-credit participation;
- Historic building age;
- Routine preventive maintenance.

It therefore provides economic context for rehabilitation, but not a direct measure of historic-preservation activity.

---

## 13. Contact and remaining uncertainties

**Census data inquiries:**  
Economic Indicators Division, Construction Expenditures Branch  
**Telephone:** 301-763-1605  
**Email:** `eid.ceb.customer.service@census.gov`  
Census also offers Construction Spending email updates.[14]

Questions worth directing to the branch before a major archival or research project:

- Is there a complete official archive of machine-readable release vintages?
- What restricted research access, if any, is available for project microdata?
- What is the current coverage of state-level tables by category and year?
- Have benchmarking or undercoverage adjustments changed since the published methodology version?
- What historical materials precede the verified 1964 series?

I did not establish a program-specific records-retention schedule, a complete budget history, or guaranteed restricted microdata availability. Those should not be inferred from public aggregate access.

---

## Sources

1. **Census Bureau, About the Survey:** purpose, geography, authority, users, products, release and revision policy.  
   https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/about_the_survey.html
2. **Census Bureau, Definitions:** construction inclusions, exclusions, and value-put-in-place concept.  
   https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/definitions.html
3. **Census Bureau, Construction Spending Methodology:** sources, sampling, estimation, coverage, response, imputation, and history.  
   https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/pdf/methodology.pdf
4. **Federal Register, November 18, 2024, Construction Progress Reporting Surveys notice:** users, public benefits, authority, voluntary status, and burden.  
   https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-11-18/html/2024-26802.htm
5. **CPRS supporting statement, Part B, 2024 submission:** governance, sampling research, response challenges, and methodological responsibilities; OMB-record mirror.  
   https://omb.report/icr/202411-0607-004/doc/148946400.pdf
6. **Reginfo, ICR 202411-0607-004:** official approval, expiration, burden, and federal-cost inventory.  
   https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202411-0607-004
7. **Census Bureau, Historical Data and Old Classification:** contemporary and predecessor-series access.  
   https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/historical_data.html  
   https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/oldtc.html
8. **Census Bureau, Previous Series and Comparison:** residential-improvement coverage variants.  
   https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/previousseries.html  
   https://www.census.gov/construction/c30/comparison.html
9. **Census Bureau, Monthly Subnational Construction Spending: Private Manufacturing:** experimental scope, historical coverage, and quality warning.

## Overall finding

**The strongest documented risks are operational disruption and agency-wide staffing losses—not wholesale removal of historical Construction Spending data.** Historical series remain listed, the core survey’s OMB approval is active through August 2028, and Census published August 2026 estimates on October 1, 2026.

Nevertheless, releases were substantially delayed during and after the 2025 government shutdown. Census has also stopped updating the program’s visualizations “until further notice.” Agency-wide departures exceed your rubric’s 1,000-person High Risk threshold.

The ratings below apply your rubric rather than estimate numerical probabilities. They distinguish **dataset-specific evidence**, **agency-wide exposure**, and **proposals that have not necessarily been implemented**. The review covers changes and disruptions since January 2025; recovered delays still count as documented disruptions.

## Preservation implications

**Preservation is warranted now, even without evidence of imminent deletion.** The most plausible failure mode is delayed publication or diminished supporting services, compounded by loss of release versions and methodological context.

Priority actions:

1. Preserve historical spreadsheets, dated release PDFs, category dictionaries, methodology, and revision notices.
2. Keep **as-published** and **latest-revised** collections separate.
3. Archive the visualization-pause notice, ICR record, and release-calendar changes.
4. Maintain independent mirrors with checksums and retrieval dates.
5. Use FRED and other redistributors as supplementary redundancy—not assumed complete copies of all categories, geographies, and release versions.

**Limitations:** This was a documentary assessment, not an exhaustive file audit. Some PDF findings rely on indexed excerpts. Staffing evidence is agency-wide and principally describes 2025 losses; current branch-level staffing and funding were not established. No numerical probability of removal can be justified from these sources.
